The incubation period for eggs of the Black-throated robin (Plesiodryas albonotata) is remarkably consistent under controlled thermal regimes. When eggs are maintained at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the altricial nestlings emerge precisely 15 days [ab = 15 days] after the onset of full incubation, a duration that aligns with expectations for a passerine of this body size. Upon hatching, the neonates are entirely dependent on biparental care and possess a wet weight of only 4.0 grams [Wwb = 4.0 grams], a modest initial mass that underscores the substantial parental investment required during the subsequent nestling phase. This initial weight is notably low compared to the ultimate wet weight for adult females, which reaches 38.6 grams [Wwi = 38.6 grams], representing a nearly tenfold increase in body mass from hatching to adulthood. This rapid ontogenetic gain reflects the high-quality arthropod diet delivered by both parents throughout the brooding period.

The developmental trajectory of the nestling progresses swiftly following hatching. Under the typical thermal conditions associated with the active metabolic phase of this species, which occur at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a defined sequence of milestones is achieved. The nestlings attain the ability to leave the nest and achieve their first flight at 12 days after hatching [tx = 12 days after hatching], a fledging age that is relatively abbreviated for a member of the Petroicidae family at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This early fledging is followed by a continued period of parental dependence, with the young remaining in close proximity to the nest site for several days while their flight muscles and foraging skills develop. The complete achievement of nutritional independence typically occurs several weeks after the initial nest departure, as the juveniles gradually learn to capture prey on their own.

Sexual maturity, marking the onset of gametogenesis and the development of functional gonads, occurs after a more extended period of somatic growth. In the Black-throated robin, puberty is reached at 36 days after hatching [tp = 36 days after hatching], a milestone that is tracked relative to the thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] that characterize its active metabolic state. This relatively rapid attainment of reproductive capability is typical of many small-bodied insectivorous passerines, which often face high adult mortality rates and thus benefit from an early onset of breeding potential. However, the actual timing of the first reproductive event is deferred considerably beyond the point of physiological puberty, as birds must first secure a territory and establish a pair bond before initiating a nesting attempt.

The first successful breeding event for this species, representing the culmination of territory acquisition and pair formation, occurs at a substantially later age. The first brood is typically produced 1.25 years after birth [tR = 1.25 years after birth], a delay that reflects the social and ecological constraints of a monogamous bird living in montane forest habitats at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This timing corresponds to approximately 456 days of age when measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Females normally produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], with each clutch containing 2 to 5 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing 2 to 5 eggs], a modest reproductive output that is compensated by extended parental care and a relatively high survival rate of fledglings. This singular annual reproductive effort is consistent with the life-history strategy of many tropical and subtropical passerines that experience stable resource availability.

Respirometry trials conducted on resting, post-absorptive individuals at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] have recorded a maximal resting oxygen consumption of 81 milliliters per hour [JOi = 81 milliliters per hour], a value that situates the Black-throated robin within the expected metabolic range for a 38.6 gram [Wwi = 38.6 gram] passerine from the Australasian region.
